units.spoken: Dueling DQN
Learn how good the situation is once, and how much each choice adds.

In the racing game Enduro, on an empty road it hardly matters which way you steer; what matters is how good the road ahead is. Can a network learn how good the road is once, instead of once for every way to steer?

The agent is the learner that picks the moves, as taught in RL Basics. A state is the agent's situation right now; a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state; a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad, as taught in RL Basics. Here the agent is a program driving in Enduro.

In Enduro the state is the screen, a move is a steering or speed press, and the reward is points for passing cars. This page uses four moves, left, right, straight and brake; the paper lists nine actions for Enduro.

An episode is one run from the start until it ends, as taught in RL Basics. Enduro is an Atari game, a racing game for the Atari home console of the 1980s, where you race and pass other cars. Each episode is one race against the clock.

Take a look at this figure. The road ahead is what matters, not the press. On an empty stretch every press scores about the same, because the road's worth is the same for all of them. The car ahead breaks the tie: it makes one press worth more than the rest, because passing it is the only move that changes what the car earns. That is the whole problem: the road's worth is shared, and only the car ahead makes one press stand out. Learn the road once, and the press is a small extra.

Figure 1 shows the road the page reasons about: the car ahead makes one press better. Take a stretch where the car ahead sits just in front: the press that passes it is the one whose score rises above the road's worth.
This page follows the paper by Wang and co-authors (2016), which introduced the dueling network.
Section one, Steering on an empty road
Learn the road once, not four times
Picture a long empty stretch of road in Enduro, the car alone with nothing to pass. The road ahead is fast, and that matters far more than which way the car steers.
How. The network learns one number for how good the road is, shared by every press, and only the small extra each press adds is learned per press.
When it works, the car knows an empty stretch is fast without relearning it for every press.

The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less, as taught in RL Basics. A policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance, as taught in RL Basics. On an empty road the return hardly depends on which way the car steers.

A state's value V of s is the return the agent expects from state s, as taught in RL Basics. A move's value Q of s and a, also called its score, is the return the agent expects if it makes action a in state s and plays on from there, as taught in RL Basics. So on an empty road every move's score is almost the road's value V.

A Q-table keeps one score for every state and move, as taught in Q-Learning. A Q-network is a neural network that takes the state and outputs one score per move, in place of the table, as taught in Deep Q-Networks. The discount gamma sets how much a reward one step later still counts, as taught in RL Basics. No table could list every road screen, so a network reads the screen instead.

Q-learning's target is the step's reward plus the discounted best score in the next state, as taught in Q-Learning. A Q-network trained with Q-learning's target is a Deep Q-Network, DQN for short. The car earns points only when it passes another car, so most targets are just the discounted best next score.
A head is the last layer of a network, the one that outputs a quantity. A plain DQN has one head with one output per move.

In a network with one head, an update changes only the played move's output directly, and the layers below the head change too; the state's worth is not learned as one shared number. The gaps between the moves' scores are tiny next to the state's worth, so a small error in the network's guesses can reorder the moves.
The dueling network keeps the shared layers that read the screen and replaces the one head with two streams, each a small stack of layers; a plain DQN is then called a single-stream network.
Each stream ends in its own head; the value head outputs one number for the state, and the other head one number per move, what that move adds.

What this picture is teaching is that the move matters only when the road makes it matter. On the empty road the scores sit almost level, because the road's worth is the same for every press and no press adds much. Put a car ahead and the scores spread: the press that passes it pulls away from the rest, while the others stay near the road's worth. The lesson is that the network should learn the road once and let the car ahead decide which press is worth more, instead of relearning the road for every press.

Figure 2 shows two road frames side by side, an empty road and a road with a car just ahead. Take the frame with a car just ahead: steering around it is the move that matters, while on the empty road no press stands out.
Section two, Value plus advantage
The score splits in two
Picture one move's score as a bar of two blocks: a tall block every move shares, the road's worth, with a small block on top that belongs to that move alone.
How. The advantage is the move's score with the road's worth taken off. The usual result is the road's worth shared by every press.
When it works, the shared block carries almost all of each score on an empty road, and only the small top blocks differ.

The per-move head is the advantage head, because it outputs each move's advantage. The greedy policy plays the top-scored move in each state, as taught in Q-Learning. On an empty road every move's advantage is near zero; with a car just ahead, the move that passes it has the largest.

Averaged over the moves, each weighted by how often the policy picks it, the advantages come to zero. The expected score under the policy is the road's worth V by definition of V, so the expected advantage cancels to zero. So a move that is better than usual must balance a move that is worse. Under the greedy policy the best move's score is the usual result itself, so its advantage is zero and every other move's is zero or below.
Equations 1 and 2 split one score into a shared part and a per-press part.
Take a look at these equations. They split one score into a shared part and a per-press part.

The advantage line. The advantage is how much better this press is than usual. The score is what the car expects to earn from this press. The road's worth is how good the screen is on its own. Minus takes the road's worth off the score. When a press scores exactly the usual result, its advantage is zero. Beating the usual result gives a positive advantage; doing worse gives a negative one. Adding the road's worth and the advantage gives the score back.
Intuitively, the advantage is what this press adds beyond the road.
Example. Take a press that passes the car ahead: its score sits above the road's worth, so its advantage is positive and the largest.

The score line. The score is the joined number the car acts on. The road's worth is the part shared by every press. The advantage is what this press adds on its own. The plus puts the two parts together into one score. Intuitively, the two parts join back into the one score.
Intuition. The second equation undoes the first: the road's worth plus the press's extra gives back the score.
Example. Take a fast stretch with a car ahead: the road's worth is high for every press, and the passing press adds the largest extra on top, so its joined score tops the rest.
Together, the two lines split one score into the road's worth and the press's extra.

Here is the split in one picture. Each move's score is a tall shared block plus a small piece of its own, and the shared block is the same for every move. The road's worth carries almost all of each score, so the moves differ only by their small pieces. That is why the network learns the road once: the tall block is learned once per screen, and only the small pieces are learned per press. The move that wins is the one whose small piece is tallest, because the totals are mostly the same block.

Figure 3 shows how little the moves differ when the road carries most of the score. Take the left bar: its teal piece is the tallest, so steering left adds the most on this screen, while braking adds the least.

sections.section: 3 How the value and advantage streams combine

units.spoken: Section three, How the value and advantage streams combine
The mean pins the split down
Picture the value head taking a little more of every score while the advantage head gives the same little back, so no move's score changes and the true split stays hidden.

How. The network subtracts the mean advantage, the average over all moves, before it adds the road's worth, so the split cannot drift. That is a plain average over the four presses, and generally not zero, unlike the policy-weighted average that is zero.
When it works, the value head settles on one number for the road, the advantage head on the small extras, and the scores stay in the same order.

Equations 2, 3 and 4 build the combined score and pin its split down. A score built from two parts can drift: the road's worth can rise while every advantage falls, and no move's score changes, so nothing in the scores says which split is true.
These equations build the combined score and pin its split down.

The plain sum line. The score is the sum of the two heads. The value head gives the road's worth, one per screen. The advantage head gives the advantage for each press. A free drift hides behind the equals sign. Shift the road's worth up and every advantage down by the same amount, and no score moves. Intuitively, the plain sum leaves the split free to drift.
Intuition. Adding the two heads plainly leaves the split free to drift, with nothing in the scores to pin it down.
Example. Take a screen where the value head rises by the same amount every advantage falls: no move's score changes, so the drift is invisible.

The mean advantage line. The mean advantage is the average of the press's extras. The press set size is four, so the average divides by four. The advantage of press b is one press's own extra. The bar means the average over the presses. The average depends on the screen alone, not on any one press. The sum gathers every press's advantage into one total. Dividing that total by four gives the ordinary average. Intuitively, one number now stands for all four advantages.
Intuition. The mean advantage is the average of all four advantages, one number for the screen.
Example. Take an empty road: every advantage sits near zero, so their plain average sits near zero too.

The combined score line. The score stands for one press's score on one screen. The road's worth lifts every press's score by the same amount. The advantage is what this press adds by itself. The mean advantage is subtracted from each press alike. Subtracting the same average cannot change the order. The subtraction fixes the split, so a rise in the road's worth shows at once. The road's worth now sits off the true value by the average. Intuitively, subtracting the average fixes the split and keeps the order.
Intuition. The combined score takes the plain average advantage off, so the split is fixed and the presses keep their order.
Example. Take a car just ahead: the passing press's advantage is large and the others are small, so the average sits between them, and after the subtraction the passing press still comes out on top.

Subtracting the max instead would give the best move an advantage of exactly zero, as in Section 2, Value plus advantage; subtracting the mean shifts every score by the same amount, so the best move's advantage is no longer exactly zero, but training is steadier.
Argmax picks the move whose score is largest, as taught in RL Basics. To steer, the car needs only the advantage stream's argmax.

This figure shows why two streams beat one head. One head must learn the road's worth separately for every move, so it relearns the same number four times and a small error can reorder the moves. Two streams learn the road once in the value stream and let the advantage stream add each press's own extra, so the moves differ only by their extras. The point is the saving: one shared number instead of four relearned ones, and the scores keep their order because the shared part cannot drift between moves.

Figure 4 shows one head against two streams: the head relearns the road per move, the streams learn it once. Take a screen the car has read: the value stream carries the road's worth once, and the advantage stream adds each press's own extra.

In Enduro the paper's saliency maps, pictures of which pixels an output depends on most, show the value stream watching the road and the horizon, while the advantage stream reacts only when a car is right ahead.

sections.section: 4 A pass through the dueling network

units.spoken: Section four, A pass through the dueling network

Picture one road frame travelling through the network: it goes into the shared layers, the value head and the advantage head read what those layers found, the average advantage comes off, and the four move scores come out.

The live network is the Q-network being trained, with weights phi, as taught in Deep Q-Networks. Replay keeps a memory of past steps, and training draws random batches from it, as taught in Deep Q-Networks. So the network keeps learning from stretches of road it drove long ago, not only from the newest one.
A remembered step is written state, move, reward, next state, the prime meaning next; on the earlier pages these were state sub t, action sub t, reward sub t plus one, state sub t plus one.

The stages show the score being built, one part at a time. The shared layers read the frame once, the value head gives the road's worth, the advantage head gives each press's extra, and the average comes off before the scores are joined. The last stage is the surprise: the value head lights even though training aims only at the played move's score, because every move's score contains the road's worth, so training one move's score trains the shared number too. That is why the dueling network learns the road faster than a single head.

Step through the six stages and watch which parts light at each one. At the last stage, notice the value head lights even though training aims only at the played move's score, because every move's score contains the road's worth. The played move's bar stays ringed through the whole pass.
This card walks Equation 4 one stage at a time.
Watch the combined score fill in, one stage at a time.

The combined score line, stage by stage. The score is the finished number the stages build. The second stage brings the road's worth, the shared part, in. The third stage adds the advantage, this press's own extra. The fourth stage subtracts the mean advantage from all the scores. The last stage joins all three parts into each score. One shared block raises every score by the same amount. Intuitively, each stage adds one part until the score is whole.
Intuition. The walkthrough shows each part of the combined score in turn, so the subtraction can be seen doing its work.
Example. Take the stage where the advantage head and the average box are lit, and the subtracted term in the line lights with them.
Together, the stages build the score from the road's worth, the press's extra, and the average taken off.

Figure 5 walks through the dueling network. Stage 1 lights the road frame and the shared layers; stage 2 the shared layers and the value head, which outputs the road-worth bar; stage 3 the advantage head, which outputs a bar per move, and the advantage term; stage 4 the advantage head and the average box, with the mean advantage term; stage 5 the value head, the move-score bars, and the average box, with the road's worth term; stage 6 the value head, the move-score bars, and the single-stream inset, where the value head lights even though training aims only at the played move's score, because every move's score contains the road's worth, so training the played move's score trains the road's worth too. Take the played move's bar: it stays ringed through the pass, and the single-stream inset lights only at the last stage.

sections.section: 5 One line joins the two streams

units.spoken: Section five, One line joins the two streams

The code below is the network from my repo, with each stream given its own layers; in the repo, one layer is shared by the trunk and both streams. It trains a dueling network on my banana collector, an agent that gathers yellow bananas and avoids blue ones in a square arena, sensing it through 37 sensor readings, so the network reads those 37 numbers, not a screen. N_READINGS is 37, the count of sensor readings; HIDDEN is 64, the width of each hidden layer; N_MOVES is 4, the count of moves.
This code builds the dueling network's two streams.
1. The shared layers read the 37 sensor readings.
2. The value stream ends in a head with an output for the state.
3. The advantage stream ends in a head with an output per move.
The forward pass joins the streams.
This code joins the two streams into the move scores.
1. The forward pass takes the readings in.
2. Each stream reads the shared features.
3. The mean advantage is subtracted before the road's worth V is added.

The target network is a slow copy of the Q-network, with weights phi prime, that computes the targets, as taught in Deep Q-Networks. Double DQN's target lets the live network pick the next move and the target network score it, as taught in Double DQN. The dueling network's target is built exactly as Double DQN builds it.

A batch is a handful of remembered steps trained on together; the loss averages how far their scores are from their targets, as taught in Deep Q-Networks. The car's network still learns from remembered stretches of road against a slow copy.
Training reuses the Double DQN target unchanged, written out in full.
This code builds the target from the live network.
1. No gradients flow while the target is built.
2. The live network picks the next move.
3. The target network scores it.
4. The target is the reward plus the discounted next score, with GAMMA as the discount, left out at the end of an episode.
5. Acting picks the top-scored move.

sections.section: 6 The value stream carrying the road

units.spoken: Section six, The value stream carrying the road
One bar carries most of each score
Picture the tool's road with many near-copy moves: every move scores almost the same, so the shared value bar carries most of each score while the advantage bars sit near zero.
Play runs both networks on the same road, and the chart shows how far each network's scores still are from the true ones.
When it works, the dueling curve stays low from the start while the single-stream curve starts high and falls to meet it.

The tool's road is a simple made-up one whose true move scores are known. With many moves, the extras are near copies of the four named moves, so even with a car ahead many moves score almost the same.

This is the payoff in one chart. The dueling curve stays low from the start because the shared value bar carries most of each score, so the network does not have to relearn the road for every move. The single-stream curve starts high and falls to meet it, because it relearns the road per move and takes longer to learn the shared part. The gap between the curves is the saving: when many moves look alike, learning the road once beats learning it once per move, and the more alike the moves are, the bigger the saving.

Run many moves first, then few, and watch the two curves. With many near-copy moves the dueling curve stays low from the start while the single-stream curve starts high and falls to meet it. Then add more cars ahead and watch the advantage bars spread as the moves start to matter.

Figure 6 shows the tool's road, the network panel, and the chart of error against training time. Take the buttons: run many moves, then few, and watch the two curves. More cars ahead means moves matter more often, so the advantage bars spread; fewer cars leave the road empty.
Section seven, Only the head changes
Training a dueling network works exactly like training a DQN.

The learning rate eta sets how big a step each update takes, as taught in RL Basics. My repo trains a dueling network on my banana collector, keeping the paper's split into a value head and an advantage head, with smaller layers and its own inputs.

This table lines up the settings for my repo and the paper side by side. The input differs: my repo reads 37 sensor readings, the paper the last 4 Atari frames. The shared layers differ too: my repo uses two layers of 64 units, the paper DQN's convolution layers. The value head is one output in my repo and a stream of 512 units then one output in the paper; the advantage head is 4 outputs in my repo and a stream of 512 units then one output per move in the paper. Both combine by mean subtraction and both use a Double DQN target, so those two rows are the same. The learning rate is the one real knob: my repo uses Adam at 5e-4, the paper slightly lower than Double DQN's, and a higher rate learns faster and less steadily. The gradient into the shared layers is unscaled in my repo and scaled by one over the square root of two in the paper, and a smaller scale steadies the shared layers. The gradient norm clip is none in my repo and 10 in the paper, and a lower clip limits jumpy updates. The pattern is that the shapes differ because the inputs differ, and only the last three rows are knobs.

Table 1 gathers the settings for my repo and the paper, with what raising and lowering each setting does. Each row names one setting, my repo's value, and the paper's value, and for the settings that are knobs the row adds what each end does. Take the learning rate row: a higher rate learns faster and less steadily.

Epsilon-greedy usually plays the top-scored move and, with chance epsilon, a random one instead, as taught in RL Basics. The paper first tests the networks on a small corridor task, where the agent starts at the bottom left of three connected corridors and must reach the top right for the largest reward, moving up, down, left, right or standing still. The corridor is small enough that every true score is known exactly, so error here means how far the network's scores sit from the true ones.
In the corridor both learn equally fast with few moves, and the dueling network's error falls faster as moves are added.

sections.section: 8 When splitting value from advantage helps

units.spoken: Section eight, When splitting value from advantage helps
Where many moves look alike
Picture a road where the car has twenty ways to steer and nineteen are near copies: the move barely matters on most screens, so learning the road once saves twenty relearnings.

How. The split helps when there are many moves with similar scores, or many states where the move does not matter, and it combines freely with Double DQN and prioritized replay, replay that draws first the steps whose scores sit farthest from their targets, so training spends its time where the network is most wrong.
When it works, one shared number carries most of every score where the moves look alike, and the extra head costs almost nothing.
Section nine, Where the split stops helping
Pinned down, or it drifts
Picture the two blocks sliding again with nothing subtracted: the road's worth and the advantages drift against each other, and the value head ends up meaning nothing.
How. Each failure has its fix in the table below: subtract the mean, scale and clip the shared gradient, and read the value head only as relative worth.
When it works, the run stays steady, the value head keeps its meaning as the road's relative worth, and the move scores still decide the steering.

This table lines up each failure with its symptom and its fix. A plain sum with nothing subtracted lets the value and the advantage drift against each other, so the value means nothing and results get poorer; the fix is to subtract the mean advantage, as in the Equation 4 card, and watch the value stay put while the scores stay ordered. Subtracting the max instead of the mean makes training less steady, because the advantages must chase every change of the best move; the fix is to subtract the mean, so the advantages stop chasing the best move. When both streams push gradients into the shared layers the updates get larger and jumpier; the fix is to scale the shared gradient by one over the square root of two and clip the gradient norm at 10. Reading the value as the true state value leads to wrong conclusions, because with the plain mean subtracted the value is off by that plain average, a constant for the screen; the fix is to read the value only as relative worth and compare move scores for decisions. The first two rows are the split drifting or chasing, the third is the shared layers getting too much gradient, and the last is misreading what the value head means.

Table 2 lists where the split stops helping, with the cause, the symptom, and the fix. Each row starts from one cause, names what the run shows, and ends with the fix, so a row reads from what went wrong to what to change. Take the plain sum row: with nothing subtracted the value and the advantage drift against each other, and the fix subtracts the mean advantage.
Section ten, Learning the move directly

So far every page has scored moves and then picked the best. The next pages learn the move directly. The state value taught here returns as the baseline each return is compared with, and the advantage as what that comparison measures. Both return in Policy Gradient Methods: in the REINFORCE method, which learns the move directly from the returns each run earns, and in the Actor-Critic methods, which pair a move chooser with a value critic.
